catalog_quote: Gisamba has two level tone phonemes: high (H) and low (L). H is marked with an acute accent (´), low is not marked graphically. As the minimal pairs in (12) show, these tones are phonologically distinctive. (12) bul 'village' vs. búl 'wrong, evil' gudug 'to appear' gudúg 'to exit' ndund 'foam' ndúnd 'vegetable' Gisamba also has a falling (F) contour tone, which is marked with a circumflex (^). No rising tones have been observed. ... Noun prefixes in Gisamba can either be H or L. Among disyllabic nouns consisting of a noun prefix and a monosyllabic noun stem, five tone patterns are observed in isolation: L-L, L-H, H-L, H-H, and L-F. ... sweep_summary: Both title-keyword items attached to samb1309 in Glottolog (Yoon et al. 2004 ToBI reliability on Switchboard; Campbell 2007 ICPhS speech-activity in telephone dialogues) were downloaded open and read: the first is American English, the second Japanese, and Glottolog's own reference pages label both as 'computerized assignment from "telephone"' to Samba [smx]. Neither says anything about Gisamba or word stress; both are silent on the catalog and rate priority none. The catalog's 'tonal' coding (Van Acker & Bostoen 2020, sec. 3.4) stands; the 2018 MA thesis already held by the project (sec. 2.4, p. 24) confirms a contrastive H/L(/F) tone system with no stress described., }. lookups used Glottolog, DOI resolver, ISCA archive and the IPA ICPhS 2007 proceedings index directly.

new_statements.quote: Kisamba has three distinctive tones, a high tone (H) which is marked with an acute accent (´), a low tone (L) which is left unmarked, and a falling tone (F) which is marked with a circumflex (^). These falling tones are the result of the contraction of the noun prefix and the stem and therefore no fundamental phonological tones, but the result of a morphophonological rule (cf. 2.5.2.). Tone appears to be phonological distinctive in Kisamba according to a few minimal pairs, see examples in (14). The tone pattern of a word is fixed when in isolation [...] The realization of tone patterns in context is generally not the same as in isolation, but an in-depth study on tone in Kisamba is needed to fully understand this
new_statements.citation: Van Acker, Sifra. 2018. A pilot study of Kisamba (Bantu, L12a, DRC): Phonology, morphology, wordlist and some texts. MA thesis, Ghent University. 207 pp.
new_statements.reading: Lexical H/L tone system with a derived falling tone; tone is contrastive (minimal pairs in (14)); no word stress or accent placement is described anywhere in the phonology chapter (a full-text search for stress/accent the full text: 'stress' absent, 'accent' only as the diacritic name). This was downloaded by the prior check pass (already held by the project) and re-read here; it is the thesis underlying the catalog's deciding 2020 article and says the same thing. Neither of the two title-keyword items in this search of works with stress in the title concerns Samba at all.

The tone patterns in Kisamba are illustrated in table 5.' and the final clause continues ', see examples in (15).' audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated pages in the held 2020 article. The classification 'tonal, no stress rule described' rests on the only peer-reviewed phonological description of the language (2020), written by the language's sole describer with her supervisor; the underlying 207-pp MA thesis was downloaded from Ghent's open repository and independently confirms a lexical H/L(/F) tone system with minimal pairs, non-phonemic vowel length, and no mention of stress or accent. No better or competing source exists (thesis sec. 1.2: no prior description; remaining Glottolog entries are misattributed non-Gisamba items). Caveat for the record, already reflected in the quote: both sources call their tone data preliminary and note isolation vs. context tone differences ('tone case'), but nothing points toward a stress analysis.
